title: World Calendar
intro: A proposed permanent world calendar in which each quarter has the same length and ordinary dates repeat their weekday pattern each year.
summary: Four quarters of 91 days each, plus a special World Day and an additional leap-year day outside the regular week.
origin: The World Calendar was proposed as a twentieth-century calendar reform for simpler recurring business and civic schedules.
structure: Every quarter has 31 days in its first month followed by two 30-day months, totalling 91 days or exactly 13 weeks.
pattern_note: World Day is added at year-end and a leap-year day follows June; these are special days outside the standard repeating weekday pattern.
history: Reformers argued that identical quarters would make accounting, business planning and annual comparisons easier. Critics objected to interrupting the continuous seven-day week.
example: The first month in every quarter has 31 days. The next two have 30 each, giving every quarter a fixed 13-week pattern.
limits: The World Calendar is a proposal, not a universally adopted civil calendar. Its intercalary days and weekday treatment should not be mistaken for Gregorian rules.
